title: Do Some Students Learn Faster Than Others?
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane surveys research on whether some students inherently learn faster than others, and finds the evidence more mixed and interesting than the 'folk knowledge' assumption that they do. A study of online learning modules found an 'astonishing regularity' in learning trajectories once controlling for wide variation in starting knowledge; a genetics study found no statistically significant link between intelligence-associated genes and learning speed; and Graham Nuthall's classroom research found students already knew about 50% of intended content going in, and that attention/engagement during class predicted with 80% accuracy what students would learn. Countervailing evidence comes from studies of complex skill learning that did find real differences in learning rate, though Kane notes these involve complex, unstructured tasks unlike typical school content broken into component skills. His synthesis: differences in learning speed shrink dramatically once teachers account for prior knowledge and break skills into small, manageable pieces.
points: Nuthall's classroom research found students already knew roughly 50% of intended lesson content before instruction began, and that observed attention/engagement predicted with 80% accuracy which ideas students would actually learn.
A genetics study of 131 people across nine cognitive measures over 100 days of learning found no statistically significant link between intelligence-associated genes and learning speed.

Countervailing evidence from mental-multiplication and air-traffic-control studies did find real differences in learning rate, but Kane notes these are complex, unstructured tasks unlike school content broken into discrete, practiced component skills.

His actionable reframe for teachers: when a student appears to learn slower, ask what specific prior knowledge they're missing and whether the skill can be broken into smaller component pieces, rather than treating the gap as innate.
quotes: The 'astonishing regularity' is that the learning trajectories look almost identical... My claim here isn't that every student learns at exactly the same rate, it's that those rates are more similar than they are different.
Students already knew, on average, about 50% of what the teachers intended to teach!

Using their observations, they could predict with about 80% accuracy which ideas students would learn... Their model didn't take into account any characteristics of the students besides what they observed directly.

I think I can make two claims: differences in student learning speed are minimized when teachers account for prior knowledge of the topic they’re teaching, and differences in student learning speed are minimized when teachers break skills down into small, manageable pieces.
My point is that the differences in learning speed are probably smaller than you think, and if you see big differences there might be some simple ways to help the students who are falling behind.
